source.title: ToddlerBERTa: Exploiting BabyBERTa for Grammar Learning and Language Understanding

record.tranche_reason: The paper varies model sizes and evaluates downstream BLiMP performance, bearing on downstream scaling behavior, but it does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream benchmark scores and statements about performance across model sizes. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute power-law fits, extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal allocations. Baseline scores are included, but cited baseline results are not treated as new scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study trains one masked-LM family at five sizes (0.75M to 92M parameters) on a 10M-word BabyLM corpus and reports BLiMP scores across sizes. This bears only qualitatively on V6, in a new low-data setting. It reports no pretraining loss, no fits and no predictions.
record.authors_conclusion: Roughly right. The authors conclude that hyperparameter choices and model size both matter. Larger ToddlerBERTa models score better on BLiMP, though smaller tuned models can beat larger baselines in the low-data regime. Their best 92M model beats the BabyLM baselines overall, using single-sentence pretraining on about 10M words.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates downstream grammar and language benchmarks rather than held-out pretraining loss; varies several architectural and training settings together and does not fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies hidden size, intermediate size, attention heads, layers, number of mask patterns, epochs, and batch size. It reports that these choices affect benchmark performance.

fits_no_version.finding: At the same 8.5M parameters, the best ToddlerBERTa-base configuration scores 0.7407 on BLiMP, versus 0.6660 for the original BabyBERTa configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In low-data masked-LM pretraining, training-recipe choices (mask patterns, epochs) change downstream grammar scores about as much as scaling model size does.

fits_no_version.finding: ToddlerBERTa-s (1.8M) beats the OPT-125M baseline on BLiMP in several configurations. ToddlerBERTa-xs (0.75M) is competitive with the T5 baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across architectures in the low-data regime, small models with a tuned recipe can outperform much larger models, so parameter count alone does not predict the downstream score.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the BabyLM Challenge at the 27th Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning
record.problems: No held-out pretraining-loss measurements or scaling-law fits are reported. Model size is varied alongside architecture and training settings, so size effects are not isolated. The text provides no uncertainty estimates for the reported comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1–5 show many individual training-configuration scores for each model size, but the extracted text does not provide reliable per-configuration numerical values. The record therefore retains the size-related results described explicitly in the prose rather than transcribing unassignable figure values.

untested.parts: Whether downstream gains are predictable (no fit or extrapolation); any link to pretraining loss; scaling of data or compute.
All parts: no held-out loss is reported.
All parts: shape is never varied at a fixed parameter count.

missing.what: Best BLiMP score per model size (xs, s, base 0.7407, l, xl 76.68), giving the size trend in numbers. Only base and xl are stated numerically in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's fits_no_version entry pointed to a nonexistent row r3; I removed that reference. The evidence is weak: there are no loss measurements and no uncertainty estimates, and size is confounded with a 36-configuration hyperparameter sweep per size. The relation is a marginal 'tests', on V6 only.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law behavior in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token counts.
The paper changes width, depth, intermediate size, and attention heads together across model configurations; it does not compare architectural details at a fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or the specified alternative training regimes are studied.
No relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is measured, and the paper does not establish a fitted or predictive performance-versus-scale relationship.
Hyperparameters are varied, but the paper does not fit scaling exponents, compare fitting choices, or test compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: ToddlerBERTa-l
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated model configurations on BLiMP and described performance relative to larger architectures.

conditions.value: varied training configurations shown in Figure 4

rows.baseline: smaller architectures; exact score not stated
rows.value: The text says a significant performance boost occurs in the majority of models when larger architectures are employed; it also describes the increase in the top score as modest.
rows.note: The paper does not give a numerical aggregate for the across-size comparison or isolate size from the other configuration changes.
rows.check: Prose only. The authors call the top-score gain from base to l 'relatively modest', while most configurations improve. Size is confounded with configuration sweeps, and the baseline should be ToddlerBERTa-base, whose best score is 0.7407.

rows.subject: ToddlerBERTa-xl
rows.stage_stated: pretrained; selected final configuration trained for 5 epochs with 20 mask patterns and batch size 64
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated configurations on BLiMP as part of the model-size experiments.

conditions.value: varied training configurations shown in Figure 5

rows.baseline: baselines with a similar parameter count; exact comparison value not stated in the text
rows.value: The text says Figure 5 verifies the authors' hypothesis of improvement with model scaling and describes the results as remarkable; the figure's exact values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The reported prose supports improvement with larger architectures, but gives no numerical scaling relation or demonstration that downstream results are predictable.
rows.check: Prose plus Table 2: the best xl model scores 76.68 on BLiMP, against 0.7407 for the best base model. The authors say Figure 5 verifies that performance improves with scale. Predictability is not shown, and the baseline should be the smaller ToddlerBERTa sizes, not similar-size external baselines.

relationships.condition: ToddlerBERTa family, 10M-word BabyLM data, BLiMP, best configuration per size (base to xl)
relationships.reason: The best BLiMP score rises with model size, from 0.7407 at 8.5M to 76.68 at 92M, and the authors say scaling verified their hypothesis (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Best BLiMP scores increased from a reported 0.7407 at 8.5M parameters to 76.68 at 92M.

relationships.reason: The authors describe the top-score gain at l as relatively modest. The gains are confounded with hyperparameter sweeps and come with no predictive fit (r1).
relationships.display_finding: The larger variant produced relatively modest top-score gains, confounded by hyperparameter sweeps and without a fitted predictive relationship.
